confessions.acoustic_environment: Concrete dispensary, steady dripping in zinc bucket, faint respirator hiss
confessions.title: On the First Ampoule of Iodine
confessions.transcript: Day fourteen. I am recording this on the spool from the electrocardiograph. If anyone finds this after the snow stops: I took the first ampoule of potassium iodide myself on the third night. There was only enough for three adults in the clinic. Two children had already presented with acute thyroid swelling. I gave the second and third ampoules to the twins from bunk six. I kept the first. I told myself a dead doctor saves no children next month. But when I swallowed the chalky water, I didn't think about next month. I thought about the taste of fresh pears. May God have mercy on my arithmetic.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Canal gatehouse, howling blizzard through broken glass, wet wool scraping
confessions.title: The Weight of Lock Four
confessions.transcript: Forty days since the blast. The colonel thinks I blew Lock 4 because he ordered it. He doesn't know I had the detonator wired two hours before his courier reached the gate. I watched the water rising toward the south silos. Four hundred tons of seed wheat. If that drowned, nobody in this valley eats in Year Two. So I dropped the spillway. The four hundred people in the low cottages had twelve minutes to climb the embankment in the dark. Some didn't make it. I still hear the sheep bleating as the mud took the pens.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Under-bunk crawlspace, child whispering, distant turbine hum
confessions.title: The Four Buttons and the Box
confessions.transcript: Dr. Vel lets me sit under the medicine table when my ears hurt from the boiler noise. She showed me the brass keys. She said each key opens a drawer with a different kind of sleep inside. One is for wounds, one is for teeth, and the smallest key is for when the coughing turns red. I told her I will learn how to turn the keys so she doesn't have to stay awake all night. She didn't say anything, but she gave me an dried apricot from her coat pocket.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Vaulted stone room, clinking brass weights, scrape of charcoal ledger
confessions.title: Why Scales Keep the Peace
confessions.transcript: They call me a vulture behind my back. They say Harlan charges four liters of clean distillate for a roll of zinc wire. Let them say it. When a man gives away wire for free, his neighbor expects bread for free. When the bread runs out, the neighbor comes back with an iron pipe. Price is the only thing that keeps men from remembering they are wolves. As long as my scale is balanced, nobody gets murdered in the market hall.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Granite crypt at -30m, rhythmic chisel tap on stone, carbide burner hiss
confessions.title: The Flaw in the Slate
confessions.transcript: I chipped the seventeenth letter off the memorial wall today. The boy's father begged me to leave it. He said his son died trying to reach the airlock handle. But the log says the boy dropped his air filter in the snow and ran back for his accordion. The wall cannot record bravery where there was only panic. If stone learns how to lie, the living will never know why they are still breathing.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Bunker command cell, cigarette lighter click, paper rustle
confessions.title: The Last Formal Order
confessions.transcript: Headquarters has been silent for sixty days. I still sign my morning reports 'Commanding Officer, Sector 9 Defense Garrison.' Who am I reporting to? The geophone clicks on 120 bpm. The soldiers are down to six hundred calories a day. Today Corporal Taras asked if we should trade our sidearms to the syndicate for salt pork. I told him the first man who sells his bayonet will be tried under Article 44. Then I went to my cot and counted my remaining nine rounds.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Roaring draft, iron shovel scraping concrete, steam rattle
confessions.title: The Singing Flue
confessions.transcript: When the wind hits minus thirty outside, the smoke pipe starts singing at 432 Hz. Sounds like a woman crying down a dry well. The green coal we got from the lower seam pops like gunfire in the firebox. My forearms are covered in blister scars from the draft blowbacks. But so long as the needle stays at six atmospheres, the little ones in bunk four don't freeze in their sleep. I shoveled twelve tons today. My spit is black as pitch.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Quiet schoolroom, chalk squeak on slate, distant coughing
confessions.title: What Must Not Be Erased
confessions.transcript: The council wanted to take the school room for cabbage storage. I stood in the doorway with my iron pointer until they brought the sacks elsewhere. If these fourteen children grow up knowing only how to shovel slag and test radon filters, what was the point of surviving? Today we learned the names of the seven oceans. None of them will ever see an ocean, but they can spell the word 'Pacific'. That is my victory.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Rhythmic hammer on anvil (60 bpm), quench tank hiss
confessions.title: Turning Spring Steel
confessions.transcript: We cut the leaf springs out of three pre-war trucks today. High manganese steel. Difficult to work with hand bellows, but it holds an edge that can cut granite. I forged twelve surgical scalpels for Dr. Vel and forty pickaxe teeth for the excavation gang. When you hit hot steel, you don't think about the fallout clouds. The iron only answers to heat and hammer. It is the only honest thing left.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Dead Hand vault -80m, telemetry beeps, cooling fan drone
confessions.title: Catalog of the Silent Frequencies
confessions.transcript: Station Zero log, day five hundred. Frequency 104.7 MHz is clear. Of the seventy-four provincial stations that were broadcasting on impact day, seventy-three are absolute static. Only 99.0 MHz remains, reading its endless census of ghosts. Last night satellite Harrow-4 dipped to one hundred ninety kilometers. I could hear its solar panels screaming against the upper atmosphere. In two hundred days, the sky will start dropping its iron.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Surface whiteout blizzard, rubber gas mask flutter, crunching frozen crust
confessions.title: The Salt Marsh Crossing
confessions.transcript: Surface temperature minus twenty-eight. Dosimeter is ticking eighty clicks a minute through the snow. I found the remains of the mail truck by Mile Post 14. The driver was still at the wheel, mummified by the freeze. In the back was a crate of dried milk and twenty letters that were never delivered. I brought the milk back. The letters I left on the dash. Some news is too old to do anyone any good.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Wood shavings rustling, hoop driver knocking on oak stave
confessions.title: The Pitch and the Oak
confessions.transcript: A water barrel is not just wood; it's five days of life for twelve people. If the staves dry out and shrink by a millimeter, forty liters of clean distillate leaks into the dirt floor while everyone sleeps. I boil the pine pitch three times to get the sulfur out before sealing the seams. My hands are black with resin. When I die, they can bury me in one of my own casks. It will be the only dry box in Tessarat.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Paper crumbling, soft page turns, slow pencil scratching
confessions.title: The Books We Burned for Heat
confessions.transcript: During the third frost week, we burned four shelves of the municipal tax registry to keep the clinic stove going. I made sure we burned the tax ledgers first. Then the judicial case files from 1974. But on Tuesday we had to burn the illustrated atlas of botanical species. I tore out the color plates of the apple orchards and hid them in my mattress. If we survive the winter, someone must remember what an orchard looks like in bloom.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Surface airlock outer door, howling wind, click of rifle safety
confessions.title: The Stranger at Three AM
confessions.transcript: A man came to the hatch at 03:00 during the ash squall. He didn't knock three times; he just beat on the iron with a stone until his gloves tore. Through the viewing slit, his dosimeter glow tube was glowing bright violet. He was carrying a sack of frozen potatoes. He begged to trade the sack for an hour inside the outer airlock. Voss told me to keep the bolts thrown. I watched the man sit down in the snow with his back to the door. By dawn, the snow had drifted over his boots.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Treadle sewing machine clicking, scissors cutting thick canvas
confessions.title: The Lead Lining
confessions.transcript: I am sewing lead foil from cigarette packages between layers of heavy wool for the scout coats. It adds eight kilograms to the shoulders, but it drops the gamma dose by twenty percent. The needle breaks on every third seam. My fingertips are bruised purple. Sonya came by today to help me thread the linen cord. She has good eyes in the candlelight. I gave her a button made of carved bone.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Dough slapping on wood table, oven draft roaring
confessions.title: The Sawdust Fraction
confessions.transcript: We are up to thirty percent sifted alder sawdust in the bread flour now. If you sift it fine enough through copper gauze, the dough rises with potato yeast, but it bakes hard as grey slate. You have to soak it in hot water before eating or it cuts the roof of your mouth. But it fills the stomach. When the belly stops cramping from emptiness, a man can work his eight hours on the sump pump without collapsing.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Foot-lathe treadle pumping, brass chip spiraling on bed
confessions.title: Turning the Valve Stem
confessions.transcript: The bronze intake valve for Pump #3 had three stripped threads. We had no replacement castings. I took a solid bronze door handle from the old bank building and spent forty hours turning it down on the foot-lathe by candlelight. Every half-millimeter cut was taken with a hand file. If the threads bind, the low reservoir overflows into the coal bunker. When I tightened the gland nut this morning, it held forty pounds of pressure without a single drop.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Boiling kettle bubbling, wooden spoon scraping tin pot
confessions.title: The Bone Broth
confessions.transcript: We have boiled the same beef femur four times this week with pine needles and dried turnip peelings. The broth is clear as river water now, with only a few drops of yellow tallow floating on top. But when the shift comes off the ice road, a hot mug in both hands stops the shivering faster than a wool blanket. I add a pinch of mineral salt and tell them it's mutton soup. They know it's a lie, but they drink it anyway.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Rhythmic breathing, snowshoe crunch on hard ice crust
confessions.title: The Eleven Kilometers
confessions.transcript: Eleven kilometers between Outpost 9 and the central bunker. In a blizzard, you cannot see your own hand on the guide wire. If your glove slips off the steel cable, you lose the skin on your palm in three seconds. I carry six letters in my oilcloth pouch and a bottle of kerosene for the lantern. When the wind hits seventy kilometers an hour, you don't pray; you just count your paces from marker stake to marker stake.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Soft breathing, turning paper pages, distant pump rhythm
confessions.title: The Garden in the Slate
confessions.transcript: Sonya showed me how to sharpen the carbon pencils with an iron rasp. We drew pictures of cabbages and red tomatoes on the underside of our bunk boards where the sergeant can't see them. She said that before the war, tomatoes grew right out of the dirt without glass roofs or radiator pipes. I don't know if that's true. But when I touch the red crayon mark, it feels warmer than the stone wall.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Water dripping on shale, pickaxe strike on rock fault
confessions.title: Shoring the Fault Line
confessions.transcript: The seismic shock from the three megaton groundburst fifty kilometers south cracked the limestone bed right through Sector 4. Every time the heavy train goes by on the surface, shale falls from the ceiling. I placed four oak timber bents and wedged them with split railway ties. The wood groans when the rock shifts, but oak will bend two inches before it snaps. A man learns to trust the sound of groaning wood.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Gentle linen folding, clink of glass dropper bottle
confessions.title: The Carbolic Wash
confessions.transcript: We have run out of clean distilled water for the wound washes. I boil the gray snowmelt twice and filter it through charcoal and crushed limestone. It leaves a white chalk residue on the bandages, but it stops the gangrene. Dr. Vel's hands were shaking today while setting a fractured collarbone. I held the splint so the patient wouldn't see. We never talk about what happens when her lungs stop.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Wind whipping tarpaulin, brass cartridge rattling in tin box
confessions.title: The Empty Perimeter
confessions.transcript: We stood watch four hours on the south intake. Nothing moved across the ash dunes except the wind rolling dead thistle bushes. You stare through the scope until your eyes water from the cold, expecting the armor columns from the southern district. But there are no columns coming. There is no army left to fight. Just forty frozen men in a hole in the ground guarding three sacks of grain.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Hum of incandescent grow lights, soft water dripping on peat moss
confessions.title: The First True Leaf
confessions.transcript: Bed number six sprouted its first true leaf of winter rye under the 40-watt ballast light. It's pale yellow, not green, because the spectrum from the wire filament lacks blue wavelengths. But the stem is straight. I tested the soil runoff with litmus paper: pH 6.4. The bone ash neutralizer worked. If we can keep the radiator pipes from freezing on Thursday, we will have thirty kilograms of grain by spring.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Diesel engine thump-thump (120 bpm), oil can pump squeak
confessions.title: The Bearings of Generator Two
confessions.transcript: The main babbitt bearing on Generator 2 wiped out at three in the morning. We couldn't cast new babbitt alloy without tin. I melted down forty antique pewter teapots from the dining hall and poured the molten metal directly into the bearing shell. We scraped the journal with a broken file until the shaft turned free. When the engine fired back up, the lights in the clinic stopped flickering. Pewter holds up just fine if you keep the tallow pumping.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Rhythmic breathing inside bronze helmet, bubbling exhaust valve, distant metal groan
confessions.title: Walking the Sovereign's Companionway
confessions.transcript: Underwater, the acid rain doesn't matter. Everything is green-black brine and silence. You walk along the drowned deck of the Sovereign, and your lead boots sink three inches into the silt. The staterooms are full of floating coats and wooden chairs bumping against the ceiling. In the galley, forty jars of canned peaches were still sitting on the iron rack, completely sealed. I brought up three jars. When we opened them on the barge, the whole harbor smelled of summer fruit.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Lathe humming, foot treadle rhythm, clink of iron wrenches
confessions.title: The Foundry Apprenticeship
confessions.transcript: I am fourteen today. Oleg gave me my own six-inch machinist's square and a pair of leather welder's gloves that fit my hands. In the morning I teach the small ones how to read the pressure gauges; in the afternoon I help turn the cupola tuyeres on the lathe. The air in the foundry smells of sulfur and burnt grease. Some days I miss Dr. Vel so much my chest aches. But her medicine box keys are in my pocket, and every drawer is organized.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Heavy stone vault, rustle of dry parchment contracts, clink of bronze coins
confessions.title: The Day One Thousand Reckoning
confessions.transcript: Day one thousand. We have retired the emergency salt vouchers and minted five hundred bronze tokens backed by the foundry's iron output. The people complain that Harlan is making money out of nothing. They don't understand that a coin is just a promise that everyone agrees not to break. When the farmer accepts the token for his potatoes, he is betting that civilization is going to last until next winter. And as long as I hold the bullion, he won't lose that bet.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Deep underground echo, stone dust scraping, slow steady mallet taps
confessions.title: The Last Line on the South Wall
confessions.transcript: The south wall of the crypt is full. Eight hundred and forty-two names carved in granite. Today I carved the final period after the name of Old Man Kroll. He lived five years after the impact, surviving on turnip soup and dry rusks, and died in his sleep with clean blankets over his feet. The new generation does not remember the optical flashes. They only know the names on this stone. That is how it should be.

confessions.acoustic_environment: Spacious assembly hall, natural wind through glass window, crowd murmuring
confessions.title: Ten Years Beyond the Ash
confessions.transcript: Ten years ago today, Dr. Vel held my hand and spoke thirty-one names before she closed her eyes. I was eight years old. I had a dead crow in a sardine tin and four buttons in my pocket. Today we opened the valley canal locks to the southern province. The water was clear enough to see the gravel on the bottom. The constitution is signed. The blast furnaces are under civil regulation. We did not just survive the atomic exchange; we built a home out of the ashes. To everyone whose name is carved in the crypt: your labor was not in vain.
